Match each mixture to the property that differs.

(A) \(H_2O/CH_2Cl_2\): two immiscible liquids; an organic solute is recovered from the aqueous layer by shaking with the immiscible organic solvent, i.e. **differential extraction** (ii).

(B) 1-tetralone / 4-nitrophenol: two organic solids of different polarity and hence different adsorption on the stationary phase, separated by **column chromatography** (iii).

(C) Kerosene / naphthalene: components of sufficiently different boiling point in a liquid mixture, separated by **fractional distillation** (iv).

(D) \(C_6H_{12}O_6/NaCl\): the two solids differ widely in solubility, so the mixture is separated by **crystallisation** (i).

Hence A-(ii), B-(iii), C-(iv), D-(i), which is option (A).

Nitrobenzene is reduced by \(H_2/Pd\) in ethanol to aniline, so \([A]=C_6H_5NH_2\).

Aniline is then acetylated by acetic anhydride in pyridine (pyridine mops up the acetic acid liberated). The nucleophilic \(-NH_2\) attacks the anhydride carbonyl, giving the anilide:

\(C_6H_5NH_2 + (CH_3CO)_2O \rightarrow C_6H_5NHCOCH_3 + CH_3COOH\)

So \([B]\) is acetanilide (N-phenylethanamide), which is the structure drawn in option (A).

Empirical formula \(C_6H_6O\) with a sooty (luminous) flame indicates a high carbon content aromatic compound, so \(A\) is phenol.

The \(-OH\) group is strongly activating and o-, p-directing. In a solvent of low polarity (\(CS_2\), \(CHCl_3\)) at low temperature the phenol is not ionised to the far more reactive phenoxide, so polybromination is avoided and monobromination occurs. Attack at the para position is preferred because the two ortho positions are sterically hindered by the \(-OH\) group.

Hence \(B\) is 4-bromophenol, option (C). (In polar water the phenoxide forms and 2,4,6-tribromophenol precipitates instead - which is why the low-polarity solvent is specified.)

\(Cu^{2+}\) oxidises iodide, and the copper is itself reduced to the +1 state because CuI is very insoluble:

\(2Cu^{2+} + 4I^- \rightarrow Cu_2I_2(s) + I_2\)

The white precipitate \(X\) is therefore cuprous iodide \(Cu_2I_2\) (the brown colour of the solution is the liberated iodine, not the precipitate).

The liberated iodine is estimated by titration with sodium thiosulphate, in which thiosulphate is oxidised to tetrathionate:

\(I_2 + 2Na_2S_2O_3 \rightarrow 2NaI + Na_2S_4O_6\)

So \(Y = Na_2S_4O_6\) (sodium tetrathionate). Hence \(X = Cu_2I_2\), \(Y = Na_2S_4O_6\), option (D). Option (C) carries the impossible formula \(Na_2S_4O_5\).

A trans alkene cannot be flipped directly, so it is taken down to the alkyne and re-reduced stereoselectively.

Step 1: \(Br_2\) adds across the double bond to give the vicinal dibromide \(Ph-CHBr-CHBr-CH_3\).

Step 2: **alcoholic** KOH is required - alcoholic KOH gives elimination, whereas aqueous KOH would only give substitution (the diol). This removes one HBr to give the vinyl bromide.

Step 3: \(NaNH_2\) (a much stronger base) removes the second HBr from the vinylic halide to give the alkyne \(Ph-C \equiv C-CH_3\).

Step 4: \(H_2\) over Lindlar catalyst adds syn across the triple bond, giving the **cis** alkene. (Na in liquid \(NH_3\) would deliver the anti addition and regenerate the trans alkene.)

Hence option (B).

(i) \(CH_3CH_2CHO + HCHO \rightarrow HOCH_2-CH(CH_3)-CHO\)

(ii) On heating, dehydration gives the conjugated enal \(CH_2=C(CH_3)-CHO\) (2-methylprop-2-enal, \(C_4H_6O\)).

The new stereocentre is created from achiral reagents by attack on either face equally, so \(B\) is a **racemic mixture** and is therefore optically inactive. Being a carboxylic acid it liberates \(CO_2\) from saturated \(NaHCO_3\).

Hence option (B). Option (C) fails because the product is racemic, not optically active.

Count the steric number (bond pairs + lone pairs) on the central atom.

A. \(XeF_4\): 4 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs, \(sp^3d^2\); the lone pairs occupy opposite axial sites, leaving a **square planar** shape (II).

B. \(SF_4\): 4 bond pairs + 1 lone pair, \(sp^3d\); the lone pair takes an equatorial position, giving a **see-saw** shape (I).

C. \(NH_4^+\): 4 bond pairs, no lone pair, \(sp^3\); **tetrahedral** (IV).

D. \(BrF_3\): 3 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs, \(sp^3d\); both lone pairs equatorial, giving a **T-shaped** molecule (III).

Hence A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III, option (D).

This is the stratospheric chlorine reservoir chemistry of ozone depletion.

The chlorine monoxide radical is mopped up by nitrogen dioxide to give chlorine nitrate:

\(ClO + NO_2 \rightarrow ClONO_2\), so \(X = ClONO_2\)

Chlorine nitrate is then hydrolysed by water (the reagent written over the second arrow):

\(S^{2-}\), \(Cl^-\), \(K^+\) and \(Ca^{2+}\) are isoelectronic - each has 18 electrons.

Within an isoelectronic series the radius falls as the nuclear charge rises, because the same 18 electrons are pulled in harder:

\(Ca^{2+}(Z=20) < K^+(Z=19) < Cl^-(Z=17) < S^{2-}(Z=16)\)

Equivalently, radius increases as the ratio (charge/electrons) becomes more negative. The increasing order is therefore \(Ca^{2+} < K^+ < Cl^- < S^{2-}\), option (C).

A surfactant molecule has an ionic/polar head and a long non-polar hydrocarbon tail, and it always arranges itself so that each end faces the medium it likes.

In **water** the tails hide inside and the polar heads face the solvent - the normal micelle.

In a **non-polar solvent** the situation inverts: the hydrocarbon tails point outwards into the solvent and the polar heads huddle together in the centre. This is the reverse (inverted) micelle, and it is the structure drawn in option (A), where the head circles form the core and the wavy tails radiate outwards.

Option (B) is the normal micelle (correct only for water), and (C)/(D) show monolayers rather than micelles.

Melting point of an isomeric solid is governed mainly by how well the molecules pack in the crystal lattice, and packing improves with molecular symmetry.

p-Dichlorobenzene is the most symmetrical of the three isomers, so it packs most tightly and needs the most energy to melt (m.p. about \(53^{\circ}C\)). The ortho and meta isomers are unsymmetrical and pack poorly, melting far lower (about \(-17^{\circ}C\) and \(-25^{\circ}C\) respectively).

So the order is para > ortho > meta, which is the sequence drawn in option (B).

(Boiling points would follow dipole moment instead, giving ortho > meta > para - that is the trap in the other options.)

Electrolysis of aqueous NaCl (brine) is the chlor-alkali process.

At the **anode** the competing oxidations are \(2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_2 + 2e^-\) and water to \(O_2\); because of the high chloride concentration and the large overpotential for oxygen, chlorine is discharged:

Anode: \(2Cl^-(aq) \rightarrow Cl_2(g) + 2e^-\)

At the **cathode** \(Na^+\) is not discharged from aqueous solution (its reduction potential is far too negative); water is reduced instead:

Cathode: \(2H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2(g) + 2OH^-(aq)\)

So hydroxide ion is produced at the cathode - option (D). \(Cl_2\) forms at the anode (not the cathode), and \(H_2\) at the cathode (not the anode), so (A), (B) and (C) are wrong.

For a one-electron species, \(\bar{\nu} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = RZ^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2}-\dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)\).

For hydrogen (\(Z=1\)) the same wavelength requires

Hypophosphoric acid is \(H_4P_2O_6\). Its structure has two equivalent phosphorus atoms joined by a direct P-P bond, each also bearing one \(P=O\), one \(P-OH\) and one bridging bond.

Using oxidation numbers on \(H_4P_2O_6\):

\(4(+1) + 2x + 6(-2) = 0\)

\(4 + 2x - 12 = 0 \Rightarrow 2x = 8 \Rightarrow x = +4\)

So phosphorus is in the \(+4\) state. (The P-P bond contributes nothing, since it is between identical atoms.)

Do not confuse this with hypo**phosphorous** acid \(H_3PO_2\), where P is \(+1\).

Examine each transformation for whether the nitrogen ends up attached directly to a benzene ring.

1. Benzamide \(+ Br_2 + NaOH\): Hofmann bromamide degradation converts \(C_6H_5CONH_2\) to \(C_6H_5NH_2\) with loss of one carbon. Aniline - **aromatic amine**.

2. Potassium phthalimide \(+\) chlorobenzene: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis proceeds by \(S_N2\) attack of the phthalimide anion on the halide. Aryl halides do not undergo \(S_N2\) (partial double bond character of the C-Cl bond, sp2 carbon, back-side attack blocked by the ring), so **no reaction** - this is exactly why Gabriel synthesis cannot make aromatic amines.

3. Nitrobenzene \(+ H_2/Pd\)-C: catalytic reduction of the nitro group gives aniline - **aromatic amine**.

4. Acetanilide \(+\) dilute \(H_2SO_4\), heat: acidic hydrolysis of the amide gives aniline (as the salt, liberated on basification) plus acetic acid - **aromatic amine**.

Three of the four give aromatic amines.

Answer: 3.
